linsen_spiegel.title: 🌈 The optics adventure 🔦
linsen_spiegel.subtitle: Welcome, young researchers! Buckle up, we're traveling on a beam of light through the exciting world of optics!

sections.title: 1. Reflection: Ping-Pong with light

quizzes.question: What is the name of the invisible guide line that stands vertically on the surface when mirrored?

answers.feedback: Not yet. The reflected ray is the outgoing light ray. For angles, use the normal as the perpendicular reference line.
Exactly. The normal is the perpendicular helper line at the hit point. Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from it.

sections.content:
Light particles often behave like perfect little bouncy balls. If you throw a bouncy ball at an angle against a smooth wall, it will bounce back the same way in the other direction. The light does exactly the same thing on a smooth mirror! In physics, this reflection is called Reflection.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Law of Reflection
To measure how obliquely the light hits the mirror, physicists paint an invisible guide line exactly perpendicular (at a 90-degree angle) onto the mirror. This line is called the Lot.
The angle between the incoming light beam and the plumb line is called Infallwinkel. The law of nature is super simple: angle of incidence = angle of reflection!

🎮 The Laser Mirror

Move the slider to aim the laser flatter or steeper at the mirror:

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. Refraction: The kink in optics

quizzes.question: Why does the light beam bend when it hits the water at an angle?

answers.text: Because the water is optically denser and slows down the light.
answers.feedback: Correct. In optically denser water, light is slower and therefore changes direction.

answers.text: Because the water is wet and washes away the light.
answers.feedback: That sounds plausible in everyday language, but not in physics. The bend comes from a different propagation speed in the medium.

sections.content:
Light is extremely fast in empty space. But when it travels through materials like water or thick panes of glass, it has to work harder and is slowed down slightly. If a beam of light enters such a material at an angle, it suddenly changes direction as it brakes. We call this Brechung!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Optical Density
Water and glass are harder to penetrate than air. They are said to have a higher optical density. Imagine running across asphalt and running diagonally into a basin full of modeling clay. The foot that first steps into the dough is immediately slowed down. The other foot continues to run quickly - this means you automatically make a curve! This is exactly how the light bends towards the plumb.

🧪 The Pelvic Laboratory

Select which material the laser beam should shine into:

Current: Air (Same density, beam just goes straight)

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. Total internal reflection: When light is caught

quizzes.question: What happens to the light beam during total reflection?

answers.text: It is completely reflected back at the interface like a mirror.
answers.feedback: Exactly. In total internal reflection, the ray stays completely in the dense medium and is reflected like at a mirror.
Not quite. Energy does not just vanish: beyond the critical angle, the ray is fully reflected.

sections.content:
Imagine you are underwater and looking diagonally up at the surface. At a certain angle something magical happens: the light can no longer leave the water! Instead, it is reflected at the surface of the water like a perfect mirror. We call this Total reflection.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Limit Angle
Total internal reflection only happens when light moves from an optically dense substance (like water or glass) into a thinner substance (like air) - and at a very shallow angle. The angle at which this happens is called limit angle.

🔦 The light in the glass rod

Move the laser. From a certain angle the light is no longer refracted, but totally reflected!

{{QUIZ_q_total}}

sections.title: 4. The Eye: Your built-in camera

quizzes.question: What does the lens of the eye do to help us see things close up clearly?

answers.text: It becomes thicker and more curved.
answers.feedback: Perfect. For nearby objects, the lens becomes more curved and gains refractive power.
That applies to far vision. For near vision, the eye needs a thicker, more curved lens.

sections.content:
Your eye works almost like a digital camera. There is a lens at the front that focuses the light and projects a sharp image onto the back wall of the eye (the retina). The crazy thing: Everything on the retina is upside down! Your brain only turns the image the right way around again.

Two types of lenses:

  • Converging lens (convex lens): It is thicker in the middle than at the edge (curved outwards). It focuses the light into one point (focal point). The magnifying glass is a typical collecting lens!
  • Diffusing lens (concave lens): It is thinner in the middle than at the edge (curved inwards, like a "cave"). It scatters the rays of light outwards as if they were flying apart.

Memory tip: Convex curves outward (like a belly). Concave curves inward (like a cave).

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Accommodation
So that you can clearly see both the cell phone right in front of your nose and the distant church tower, your eye can deform the lens. Muscles flatten them (for distance) or make them thick (for close). This trick is called accommodation.

👁️ The vision simulator

Your eye adapts: click on the objects to see how the lens deforms!

Choose a distance!

{{QUIZ_q_auge}}

sections.title: 5. Lenses: light bundlers and diffusers

quizzes.question: Which lens do you use if you want to concentrate the sun's light in one point like with a magnifying glass?

answers.feedback: Yes. A convex lens focuses parallel light into the focal point, like a magnifying glass.
Close. A concave lens spreads light outward and cannot collect it in a real focal point.

sections.content:
We use refraction by shaping glass into precise curved forms. These pieces of glass are called lenses. They are used in magnifiers, glasses, and cameras.

📖 Two shapes, two tricks:
- Collecting lens (convex lens): It is nice and thick and bulbous in the middle. It captures light rays and directs them inward until they all meet in one super-hot spot: the focal point (focus).
- Diffusing lens (concave lens): It is thinner in the middle than at the edge. It pushes the rays outwards as if they were being scattered.

💡 Memory tip: Convex = curved outwards. Concave = curved inwards (like a cave).

🔍 The lens changer

Click to replace the lens:

Converging lens (convex): Focuses all rays at the focal point!

🎥 High-Quality Animation: Refraction at a converging lens

sections.title: 4. Diffraction: Light goes around the corner!

quizzes.question: When does light bend most strongly into new circular waves?

answers.text: When the gap is extremely narrow.
answers.feedback: Exactly. A narrow slit causes strong diffraction: behind the slit, light spreads sideways.

answers.text: When the gap is open like a giant barn door.
answers.feedback: The other way around: with a wide slit, the beam stays mostly straight. Strong diffraction appears with a narrow slit.

sections.content:
We previously thought that light rays only travel stubbornly straight ahead. But surprise: light actually behaves like a wave in the ocean! When this light wave hits an extremely tiny obstacle or a very narrow gap, it shows its magical nature.

📖 The clever dictionary: The diffraction (Huygens' idea)
The scientist Christiaan Huygens discovered the Huygens principle. He said: Every tiny point of a light wave can create a whole new spherical wave! If a gap is extremely narrow, we force the light through there. Suddenly the tiny gap looks like its own little lamp, and the light spreads out in a circle behind it. This is called Diffraction.

🌊 The diffraction lab

Click on the box to gradually narrow the gap:

Wide slit: The light passes through almost exclusively as a straight wave (wave front).

{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 5. Curved Mirrors: The Funhouse Cabinet

quizzes.question: Which outwardly curved mirror is often hanging at dangerous street intersections because it allows you to see a very wide field?

answers.feedback: That is the focusing mirror. For a wide field of view at intersections, you need an outward-curved convex mirror.
Correct. Convex mirrors provide a wide field of view, so they are used at intersections and in stores.

sections.content:
Thick glass lenses are often quite heavy! Sometimes we simply use curved mirrors made of metal. They behave surprisingly similarly to our lenses.

📖 The mirror-lens twin:
- Hollow mirror (concave mirror): Light falls into the recess like a soup spoon. It behaves like a converging lens! It focuses the light in front of it into a real focal point.
- Bulging mirror (convex mirror): The light hits the round "belly" (like a Christmas tree ball). It behaves like a diverging lens. The light fans out and creates a virtual focal point for our eyes that appears to be behind the mirror!

🪞 The Mirror Cabinet

Click to flip the mirror:

Hollow mirror (concave): Focuses the light like a converging lens.

{{QUIZ_q5}}

sections.title: 6. The microscope: journey to the smallest animals

quizzes.question: How many lenses does a simple microscope need at least?

answers.feedback: Exactly. A simple microscope works with an objective lens and an eyepiece.
Not quite. A single lens is more like a magnifier. A microscope needs at least two lenses.

sections.content:
To observe bacteria or cells, we place two lenses in a long tube. The lower lens near the specimen is the objective. The upper lens near the eye is the eyepiece.

📖 The Invisible Image:
The lens collects the light from the tiny sample and projects an upside-down, enlarged Intermediate image floating freely in the middle of the tube. The eyepiece now acts like a powerful magnifying glass that we point at this floating image. If the intermediate image is exactly in the violet focal point of the eyepiece, the image in the eye becomes razor-sharp!

👁️ View through the eyepiece

Out of focus!

💡 Focus tip: First adjust controller 1 until the gray intermediate image lies well in the tube. Then slide controller 2 until the purple focus point exactly touches the intermediate image!
{{QUIZ_linsen_s6_q0}}

sections.title: 7. The telescope: look at the stars

quizzes.question: What two parts does the famous Newton telescope (reflector) use to direct light into our eyes?

answers.text: A large primary mirror and a small secondary mirror.
answers.feedback: Correct. In a Newton telescope, the primary mirror collects the light and the secondary mirror redirects it to the eyepiece.

answers.text: A concave lens and a convex lens.
answers.feedback: That describes a lens system. A Newton telescope is a reflector with two mirrors.

sections.content:
A telescope for astronomers doesn't have to have an incredibly high magnification. More importantly, it collects as much faint starlight as possible! For this you need a telescope with a huge aperture.

📖 Why mirrors win over lenses:
The classic refracting telescope (we call it Refractor) uses glass lenses. But gigantic lenses weigh tons! The glass is flattened under its own weight and the image deforms. In addition, thick lenses create ugly color errors (rainbow edges) at the edges.
That's why Isaac Newton built the first mirror telescope (reflector). At the very back of the tube there is a huge, curved main mirror made of metal. It focuses the light forward, where a small, slanted secondary mirror throws the light sideways into the eyepiece. Perfect for giant observatories!

🔭 The Observatory

questions.question: 1. What is the first law of reflection (mirroring) of light?

answers.text: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
answers.feedback: Perfect. That is the law of reflection.

answers.text: Angle of incidence = half angle of reflection.
answers.feedback: Not correct. At a mirror, the angle of incidence and angle of reflection are equal.

questions.question: 2. What is the “plumb” in optics?

answers.text: An invisible guide line that is vertical (90 degrees) on a mirror.
answers.feedback: Exactly. The normal stands at 90° to the surface and serves as the angle reference.
No. In optics, the normal is an imaginary line, not a tool.

questions.question: 3. Why does a light ray bend (refract) when it dives diagonally from air into water?

answers.text: Because water has a higher optical density and slows down light.
answers.feedback: Correct. The direction change comes from lower light speed in the denser medium.

answers.text: Because the water contains small lentils.
answers.feedback: Close, but wrong. The reason is changed propagation speed, not lenses in water.

questions.question: 4. You hold a “converging lens” in your hand. How is it shaped?

answers.text: Convex (like a bulbous witch's back, thick in the middle).
answers.feedback: Correct. A converging lens is convex and thicker in the middle.

answers.text: Concave (like a cave, thin in the middle).
answers.feedback: Not quite. That shape describes a diverging lens.

questions.question: 5. What happens when straight rays of light hit a diverging lens (concave lens)?

answers.text: They gather at the focal point.
answers.feedback: That is the effect of a converging lens.

answers.text: They are pushed outwards and scattered.
answers.feedback: Exactly. A concave lens makes rays spread apart.

questions.question: 6. Mr. Huygens discovered diffraction. What did he mean by that?

answers.text: That lenses can bend when they are warm.
answers.feedback: That has nothing to do with diffraction.

answers.text: That light is like a wave and forms new circular waves after tiny gaps.
answers.feedback: Correct. With a narrow slit, light spreads sideways like a wave.

questions.question: 7. A wave of light hits a wall with an opening. At which opening is the diffraction most visible?

answers.feedback: With a large opening, the wave stays almost directional.

answers.text: With a tiny, extremely narrow gap.
answers.feedback: Exactly. The narrower the slit, the stronger the diffraction.

questions.question: 8. Which mirror behaves exactly like a bulbous converging lens and creates a true focal point?

answers.feedback: Correct. A concave mirror focuses and has a real focus.

answers.text: The flat mirror in the bathroom.
answers.feedback: A flat mirror does not create a focal point.

questions.question: 9. Convex mirrors are often hung in supermarkets and at street intersections to provide a wide field of vision. How do these work?

answers.text: They scatter light like a diverging lens; the focus appears to be at the back of the mirror.
answers.feedback: Exactly. Convex mirrors spread rays and widen the field of view.
That is the effect of a concave mirror, not a convex mirror.

questions.question: 10. We look into a microscope. What is the name of the lens that lies at the bottom near the tiny sample?

answers.feedback: Correct. The objective lens is close to the specimen.
The eyepiece is the lens near the eye, not near the specimen.

questions.question: 11. The lens in the microscope projects the enlarged sample animal into the middle of the empty tube. What do physicists call this floating image?

answers.feedback: Exactly. This first enlarged image is called the intermediate image.
Not correct. "Shadow image" is not the correct technical term here.

questions.question: 12. When do we see the image in the eyepiece crisp and relaxed when using a microscope?

answers.text: When the lens touches the eyepiece.
answers.feedback: Then it becomes blurry and hard to focus.

answers.text: When the intermediate image is exactly at the focal point of the eyepiece.
answers.feedback: Correct. It is sharp when the intermediate image and eyepiece focus match.

questions.question: 13. A classic telescope with large glass lenses is technically called...?

answers.feedback: Exactly. Refractor = lens telescope.
A reflector is a mirror telescope.

questions.question: 14. What is the small, 45-degree slanted mirror in a Newtonian reflector telescope called?

answers.feedback: Correct. The secondary mirror redirects the light sideways into the eyepiece.
That term is not used here.

questions.question: 15. Modern, gigantic astronomy telescopes are reflector telescopes. Why not build them with massive lenses?

answers.text: Because gigantic lenses are too heavy, deform and produce nasty color errors (rainbow edges).
answers.feedback: Exactly. Large lenses are heavy, deform, and cause chromatic errors.

answers.text: Because mirrors make the light in space look more colorful and pretty.
answers.feedback: No. The main reason is weight, deformation, and optical errors in large lenses.

optik1.title: 🌑 Light & Shadow 🔦
optik1.subtitle: Why are there shadows? Why does the moon change shape? Here you can find out everything about the journey of light through space and time!

sections.title: 1. How light travels

quizzes.question: In what form does light normally travel?

answers.feedback: Close — light can scatter or refract, but in a uniform medium it travels in straight lines.
Exactly. In the same medium, light propagates in straight lines.

sections.content:
Light is like a super-straight ruler. As long as nothing stands in its way, it whizzes straight through the room. But if an opaque body (like you, a tree or a stone) stands in the way, the light cannot get past there. Behind it there is an area without light: the Shadow.

🔦 The shadow simulator (point light)

Move the obstacle:

{{QUIZ_o1_s1_q1}}

sections.title: 2. Umbra and penumbra

quizzes.question: What is the penumbra?

answers.text: The area where only the light from one of two lamps reaches.
answers.feedback: Correct. A penumbra forms when at least one light source still reaches the point.

answers.text: The area where no light reaches at all.
answers.feedback: That would be the umbra. In a penumbra, some light still arrives.

sections.content:
What happens if we use two lamps? Each lamp casts its own shadow. Where both shadows overlap, it is pitch black - this is the core shadow. In the gray areas next to it there is still a bit of light from one of the two lamps - this is the Penumbral.

💡 The Two Lamp Experiment

{{QUIZ_o1_s2_q1}}

sections.title: 3. Shadows in space: eclipses

quizzes.question: What happens during a solar eclipse?

answers.text: The earth casts its shadow on the sun.
answers.feedback: Swapped: in a solar eclipse, the Moon blocks sunlight toward Earth.

answers.text: The moon casts its shadow on the earth.
answers.feedback: Exactly. The Moon is between the Sun and Earth and casts its shadow on Earth.

sections.content:
Planets and moons also cast huge shadows. During a solar eclipse the moon moves in front of the sun and casts its umbra onto the Earth. During a lunar eclipse the moon passes through the shadow of the Earth.

🌑 Solar Eclipse Model

Move the moon until its shadow hits the Earth:

🌕 Lunar Eclipse Animation

The Earth is between the sun and the moon. The moon plunges into Earth's huge shadow.

{{QUIZ_o1_s3_q1}}

sections.title: 4. Reflection: The echo of light

quizzes.question: What is the law at the mirror?

answers.text: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
answers.feedback: Perfect. For a mirror: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.

answers.text: Angle of incidence = angle of perpendicular.
answers.feedback: Not quite. Both angles are measured from the normal, and they are equal.

sections.content:
When light hits a smooth surface (mirror), it bounces off. The following applies: The angle at which the light arrives (angle of incidence) is exactly the same size as the angle at which it bounces away (angle of reflection). The light is scattered on rough walls - that's why a wall doesn't reflect.

🪞 Mirror Simulator

Angle: 45°

{{QUIZ_o1_s4_q1}}

sections.title: 5. Diffraction: When light becomes a wave

quizzes.question: What happens in a very narrow gap?

answers.feedback: No, it does not disappear. Behind a narrow slit, light diffracts.

answers.text: The light spreads out in a circle behind it (diffraction).
answers.feedback: Correct. At narrow openings, light spreads out in a fan shape (diffraction).

sections.content:
On very narrow edges, light shows its wave nature. Christiaan Huygens discovered: Every point on a wave can emit new spherical waves. The light therefore "bends" around obstacles to a certain extent (diffraction).

🌊 The diffraction lab

Click above! Wide gap: light passes straight through.

{{QUIZ_o1_s5_q1}}

questions.question: How does light propagate from a point light source?

answers.feedback: Not quite. In a uniform medium, light travels in straight lines.
Correct. From a point source, straight rays spread out in many directions.

questions.question: What do you need for a shadow?

answers.feedback: Exactly. Without a light source and an opaque object, no clear shadow forms.
A mirror is not required. What matters is a light source plus an opaque object.

questions.question: What shadow is in the middle of two lamps?

answers.feedback: Correct. In the center, the blocked regions of both lamps overlap: umbra.
That is the edge region. With the right setup, the center is the umbra.

questions.question: What happens to the shadow as the object moves closer to the lamp?

answers.feedback: The other way around: moving closer to the lamp makes the shadow larger on the screen.
Correct. The shadow grows because the light cone spreads more.

questions.question: Who casts the shadow on Earth during a solar eclipse?

answers.feedback: The Sun emits the light — here the Moon casts the shadow onto Earth.
Exactly. In a solar eclipse, the Moon is between the Sun and Earth.

questions.question: What is in the middle of a lunar eclipse?

answers.feedback: Close. In a lunar eclipse, Earth is between the Sun and Moon.
Correct. Earth blocks sunlight and its shadow reaches the Moon.

questions.question: Is the moon a light source?

answers.feedback: Exactly. The Moon does not shine by itself; it reflects sunlight.
Not quite. The Moon is not its own light source.

questions.question: What is the law of reflection?

answers.feedback: 90° is not a general law. The rule is: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.

answers.text: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
answers.feedback: Correct. Both angles are measured from the normal and are equal.

questions.question: Why doesn't a rough wall reflect?

answers.feedback: Darkness is not the main reason. Surface roughness scatters light in many directions.
Correct. Diffuse reflection prevents a sharp mirror image.

questions.question: How fast is the light?

answers.feedback: 340 m/s is about the speed of sound in air, not the speed of light.
Correct. Light is extremely fast: about 300,000 km per second.

questions.question: What do you call the 'turning the corner' of light?

answers.feedback: Refraction is direction change when light passes between media. Here, diffraction is meant.
Correct. Bending "around corners" at edges or slits is called diffraction.

questions.question: Who discovered the wave principle (spherical waves)?

answers.feedback: Newton was important, but the wavelet principle goes back to Huygens.
Correct. Huygens described light with the principle of wavelets.

questions.question: When will we see a red blood moon?

answers.feedback: No, this does not happen every night — only with a special alignment.
Exactly. The red blood moon appears during a total lunar eclipse.

questions.question: What do you call light that you can't penetrate?

answers.feedback: Correct. Opaque materials do not let light pass through.
Transparent means see-through — the opposite of opaque.

questions.question: What color do most stars shine?

answers.feedback: Not quite: stars are light sources themselves and emit their own energy.
Reflection explains planet light, but stars emit their own light.

rechenbeispiele.title: 🧮 The great physics computing adventure 🚀
rechenbeispiele.subtitle: Number juggler, the warm-up phase is over! Get out your calculator. Now we calculate, convert and put physics to the test!

sections.title: 1. SI Units: The Time Machine
sections.content:
In physics we almost always calculate time in the base quantity seconds (s). If you get a task that says minutes or hours, you have to convert it first!

💡 Conversion tip:
1 minute = 60 seconds
1 hour = 60 minutes = 3,600 seconds (60 * 60)

⏱️ Convert film time

You are watching an exciting science fiction film that lasts exactly 2.5 hours. How many seconds did you spend watching TV?

sections.title: 2. Basic sizes: Baggage control (mass)
sections.content:
Masses are preferably given in kilograms (kg). However, things are often labeled in grams (g). To know how heavy everything is together, you have to bring everything to the same unit!

💡 Conversion tip:
1,000 grams (g) = 1 kilogram (kg)
Example: 500g = 0.5kg

🧳 Pack your suitcase

You pack your suitcase for your vacation. You have clothes (12.5 kg), shoes (800 g), books (1,200 g) and a toiletry bag (0.5 kg).
How many kilograms (kg) does your suitcase weigh in total?

sections.title: 3. Prefixes: The laser measuring device
sections.content:
Kilo means thousand (1,000), milli means one thousandth (0.001). When you add lengths, they must have the same prefix, otherwise there will be chaos!

📏 The Bridge Repair

A bridge is actually 2.4 kilometers (km) long. A piece of 350 meters (m) needs to be repaired.
How many meters (m) of the bridge are still completely fine?

sections.title: 4. Formulas: The speed camera (v = s / t)
sections.content:
Now it's getting serious! The formula for speed is v = s / t (speed = distance / time). Sometimes you have to change the formula:
Calculate distance: s = v * t
Calculate time: t = s / v

🏎️ Speed camera task 1: How fast?

A cheetah sprints a distance of s = 120 meters in exactly t = 4 seconds.
Calculate its speed (v) in m/s!

v = m/s

🚀 Speed camera task 2: How far?

A cyclist rides constantly at v = 5 m/s. It travels for t = 12 seconds.
What distance(s) does he travel? (Hint: s = v * t)

s = m

sections.title: 5. Evaluate diagrams: math with pictures
sections.content:
A path-time diagram (s-t diagram) shows you how far an object has come at a certain time. You can read numbers from these lines and calculate them!

📈 Read the graph

Read from the diagram above: What is the distance s after 10 seconds?
Now calculate the speed v in m/s!

v = m/s

sections.title: 🎓 The master exam of calculations

quizzes.question: 1. How many meters are 3.5 kilometers?

answers.feedback: Correct: 3.5 km × 1000 = 3500 m.
Remember the factor 1000: 3.5 km is 3500 m, not 350 m.

quizzes.question: 2. Convert 2 hours to seconds.

answers.feedback: Not enough: 2 hours are 2 × 3600 = 7200 s.
Exactly: 1 h = 3600 s, so 2 h = 7200 s.

quizzes.question: 3. v = 20 m/s, t = 5 s. How long is the distance s? (s = v * t)

answers.feedback: That divides instead of multiplies. Use s = v × t = 20 × 5 = 100 m.
Correct: s = v × t = 20 m/s × 5 s = 100 m.

quizzes.question: 4. s = 200 m, v = 10 m/s. How long do you need? (t=s/v)

answers.feedback: Divide by the speed: t = s / v = 200 m / 10 m/s = 20 s.
Exactly: t = s / v gives 200 / 10 = 20 s.

quizzes.question: 5. How many kg is 250 g?

answers.feedback: Correct: 250 g is one quarter of 1000 g, so it is 0.25 kg.
The decimal point moved too far: 250 g is 0.25 kg, not 2.5 kg.

quizzes.question: 6. You have 1.5 meters of string. How many millimeters (mm) is that?

answers.feedback: Remember the factor 1000: 1.5 m is 1500 mm.
Correct: 1.5 m × 1000 = 1500 mm.

quizzes.question: 7. A car travels 150 km in 3 hours. Calculate v in km/h!

answers.feedback: Exactly: 150 km in 3 h gives v = 150 / 3 = 50 km/h.
You must divide by the time. Average speed is 150 / 3 = 50 km/h.

quizzes.question: 8. 💡 Pro question: To convert from km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6. How many m/s is 36 km/h?

answers.feedback: That is a common mix-up. Divide 36 km/h by 3.6 to get 10 m/s.
Correct: km/h to m/s means divide by 3.6: 36 / 3.6 = 10 m/s.

quizzes.question: 9. s = 50 m, t = 10 s. What speed is this?

answers.feedback: You missed the division by time: v = 50 m / 10 s = 5 m/s.
Exactly: distance divided by time gives 50 / 10 = 5 m/s.

quizzes.question: 10. One piece of luggage weighs 4 kg. You take out 500 g. What does it weigh now?

answers.feedback: Subtract correctly: 500 g is 0.5 kg, so 4 kg - 0.5 kg = 3.5 kg.
Correct: after taking out 0.5 kg, 3.5 kg is left.

sections.content:

sieinheiten.title: SI units: measuring, converting, understanding
sieinheiten.subtitle: Learn how physicists clearly state quantities: numerical value plus unit.

sections.title: 1. Measure: numerical value plus unit

quizzes.question: Why do scientists around the world use the SI units?

answers.feedback: Not quite. SI units are used for clear measurements, not because they sound nicer.

answers.text: So that everyone means exactly the same length, time or mass and there are no errors.
answers.feedback: Correct. SI gives scientists the same units for length, time, mass and more.

sections.content:
This is what you will learn in this topic:
  • Read measured quantities as value + unit.
  • Choose suitable units for everyday situations.
  • Convert meters, centimeters, kilometers, grams, kilograms, seconds and minutes.
  • Understand simple formulas and diagrams in physics.

When measuring, you always need two parts: a number and a unit. Only 20 is not clear. 20 cm, 20 s and 20 kg mean completely different things.

Remember: Measured value = number + unit. Example: Length = 2.1 m.

The Tape Measure Challenge

Measure the blue rectangle. Compare a fixed unit with body-based units that vary by person.

Length = ?

Unit Lab

Choose an object and then the unit that fits best.

Tip: Ask first: What is being measured?

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. The 7 basic sizes: The foundation

quizzes.question: Which unit belongs to the basic quantity “mass”?

answers.feedback: Correct. The SI base unit for mass is the kilogram (kg).
No. The second is the SI base unit for time, not mass.

sections.content:
A size tells what is being measured. A unit says what is being measured with. There are seven SI base quantities in physics. Length, mass and time are particularly important for your everyday life.

The team of 7

Click on a card and read the size, unit and unit symbol.

Choose a card.

Measure time

Click start and stop as close as possible to 2.00 s. Pay attention to numerical value and unit.

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. Prefixes and conversions

quizzes.question: How many grams are in a kilogram (kg)?

answers.feedback: No. 100 grams is only one tenth of a kilogram.
Correct. Kilo means one thousand, so 1 kg = 1,000 g.

sections.content:
Prefixes are prefixes before a unit. They help to write very large or very small values ​​briefly. The important thing is: you always convert within the same type of size. Length remains length, mass remains mass, time remains time.

Important conversions:
Length1 km = 1000 m
1 m = 100 cm
1 cm = 10 mm
Mass1 kg = 1000 g
Time1 min = 60 s

Rule: If the unit gets smaller, the number gets bigger. If the unit gets bigger, the number gets smaller.

The Unit Zoom

Slide from very small to very large.

Base: big step, table height, height.

Conversion Training

Calculate and check immediately. You can use comma or period.

Choose a task and check your answer.

sections.title: 4. Formulas: distance, time, speed

quizzes.question: What happens to your speed if you suddenly need MUCH MORE time to do the same route?

answers.feedback: Correct. More time for the same distance means a lower speed.
No. If the distance stays the same and time increases, speed decreases.

sections.content:
Formulas briefly show how quantities are related. Speed is about three quantities: Distance s, Time t and Speed v.

v = s / t

Formula Triangle

Choose what you are looking for. The triangle helps you with the change.

I'm looking for v: divide path by time. v = s / t

The Formula Speedster

Change path and time. Watch the speed change.


v = 100 m / 10 s = 10.0 m/s

This is very fast.

{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 5. Diagrams: Tables become curves

quizzes.question: Which axis in a diagram is usually horizontal on the ground?

answers.feedback: No. The y-axis usually runs vertically.
Correct. The x-axis usually runs horizontally.

sections.content:
A diagram makes numbers visible. At the bottom is usually the x-axis, for example time. The y axis goes up, for example the height.

Table -> Points -> Curve

diplom.title: 🎓 The exact measurement and math diploma

questions.question: 1. What does the abbreviation "SI" mean in the system of units?

answers.feedback: Correct. SI comes from the French name for the International System of Units.
Funny idea, but SI means the International System of Units.

questions.question: 2. In which SI unit is length measured?

answers.feedback: Correct. Length is measured in meters (m).
Feet are used in some places, but they are not SI base units.

questions.question: 3. What is the basic unit of time in physics?

answers.feedback: An hour is useful in daily life, but it is not the SI base unit.
Correct. The SI base unit for time is the second (s).

questions.question: 4. What does the prefix “Kilo” mean?

answers.feedback: That is milli, not kilo.
Correct. Kilo means one thousand times as much.

questions.question: 5. How many meters are in a kilometer?

answers.feedback: No. 100 m is only 0.1 km.
Correct. One kilometer has 1,000 meters.

questions.question: 6. What does the prefix “milli” mean (e.g. in millimeters)?

answers.feedback: Correct. Milli means one thousandth (0.001).
No. Milli makes a unit smaller, not larger.

questions.question: 7. What does the letter “v” often stand for in physical formulas?

answers.feedback: No. Lowercase v usually means speed; volume is often uppercase V.
Correct. v stands for speed, from the Latin velocitas.

questions.question: 8. What is the formula for speed?

answers.feedback: No. Adding distance and time does not give a speed.

answers.text: v = s / t (distance divided by time)
answers.feedback: Correct. Speed is distance divided by time: v = s / t.

questions.question: 9. In a graph there is the x-axis and the y-axis. Where is the y-axis?

answers.text: It is the vertical line (goes from bottom to top).
answers.feedback: Correct. The y-axis is the vertical axis.

answers.text: It is the horizontal line on the ground.
answers.feedback: No. That is the x-axis; y runs vertically.

questions.question: 10. If you run 10 meters in 2 seconds. How fast are you (v = s / t)?

answers.feedback: Correct calculation: 10 m / 2 s = 5 m/s.
You multiplied instead of dividing. For v = s/t, divide distance by time.

waermelehre.title: 🔥 The heat adventure 🌡️
waermelehre.subtitle: Hello fire tamers! Get ready, we're exploring the hot (and cold) world of temperature!

sections.title: 1. What is heat? The big tremor!

quizzes.question: What happens to the smallest particles of an object when you heat it up strongly?

answers.text: They move much faster and wilder.
answers.feedback: Correct: higher temperature means stronger particle motion.
No. When heated, particles do not stop; they move faster.

sections.content:
🎥 High-Quality Animation: Temperature as Movement

Cold means slow particles. Hot means they run around wildly and need more space!

Whether it's water, wood or air - everything around us consists of tiny little building blocks, the particles. And these particles never sit still! They shake and shake all the time. Heat is actually nothing other than movement! The hotter something is, the wilder and faster the particles race around (this is measured with a thermometer in °C). When it gets cold, they move very slowly.

📖 The smart dictionary: The absolute zero point
Is there a point at which the particles freeze completely and no longer move at all? Yes! This is called the “absolute zero point”. It is ice cold -273.15 degrees Celsius. It doesn't get colder in the entire universe!

🔬 The particle microscope

Turn up the temperature and watch the particles go crazy!

Temperature: 10°C (Cold)

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. Heat conduction: The fast spoon rally

quizzes.question: Why do people often use wooden spoons instead of metal?

answers.text: Because wood conducts heat better into the soup.
answers.feedback: No. Metal conducts heat well, so a metal handle gets hot quickly.

answers.text: Because wood is an insulator and the handle doesn't get hot, so you won't burn your fingers.
answers.feedback: Correct: wood conducts heat poorly and protects your hand.

sections.content:
When you stir hot cocoa, the handle of the spoon will eventually become warm. Why? The fast, hot particles in the cocoa push the particles at the bottom of the spoon. These push their neighbors and so the “wiggle energy” travels up the spoon. This is called heat conduction.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Conductors and Insulators
- Good heat conductors: Metals (such as copper or iron) conduct heat extremely quickly. That's why cooking pots are made of metal!
- Poor heat conductors (insulators): Wood, plastic or air hardly allow heat to pass through. That's why a winter jacket has lots of thick air cushions - so that your body heat doesn't escape!

☕ The hot soup experiment

We stick a metal spoon and a wooden spoon into hot soup. Click "Heat"!

Everything is still cold.

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. Heat radiation: heat without contact

quizzes.question: Why do houses in very hot southern countries often have white walls?

answers.text: Because you can clean white better.
answers.feedback: No. Cleaning is not the reason; light surfaces reflect much radiation.

answers.text: Because the white color repels (reflects) the heat radiation from the sun.
answers.feedback: Correct: white reflects more sunlight and stays cooler.

sections.content:
Do you remember the vacuum in space (without air particles)? How does the sun's heat come to us on Earth if there is nothing there that could "conduct" the heat? The answer: heat radiation (infrared light)! Like light, it travels rapidly through empty space and warms us up as soon as it hits our skin.

📖 Colors make the difference: Black vs. White
Dark things (like a black T-shirt) "swallow" the heat radiation (absorption) and quickly become extremely hot. Bright things (like white snow) reflect the rays like a mirror (reflection) and stay cooler.

☀️ The Parking Lot Test

The sun is shining! Which car gets hotter to get into more quickly in summer?

Black: 20°C

White: 20°C

{{QUIZ_q3}}

sections.title: 4. Heat flow: Why warm air can fly

quizzes.question: You feel the heat much more strongly above a burning candle than next to it. Why?

answers.feedback: No. The flame points upward because warm air rises; that is not the cause itself.

answers.text: Because the heated air becomes lighter and rises (heat flow).
answers.feedback: Correct: warm air becomes less dense and rises.

sections.content:
Warm particles move faster and take up more space. This causes hot air to expand and become “lighter” than the cold air around it. What happens? The warm air rises! This is called heat flow (or convection). Cold air sinks downwards.

📖 The Hot Air Balloon Secret
A hot air balloon has no engine! The pilot just fires a huge gas burner. The air in the huge shell becomes hot, expands and pulls the basket into the sky as if by magic. If the air is allowed to cool, the balloon will sink again.

🎈 The Balloon Ride

Hold the button (or click multiple times) to light the burner!

{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 5. States of aggregation: ice, water, steam!

quizzes.question: What is the process called when liquid water turns into invisible water vapor?

answers.feedback: No. Condensation is gas turning into liquid, like fog on a mirror.
Correct: liquid turning into gas is called evaporation.

sections.content:
Heat can completely transform things! Almost every substance has three appearances (states of aggregation): solid, liquid and gaseous. This is again due to our particles! When they are completely cold, they cuddle close together and are rigid (ice). If it gets warmer, they loosen and flow around (water). If it gets really hot, they fly wildly apart into the air (water vapor).

📖 The magic words of physics:
- Solid to liquid = Melting (Snowman in the sun)
- Liquid to gaseous = Evaporating (Boiling Pasta Water)
- Gaseous to liquid = Condensation (mirror fogs up when showering)

💧 The Water Machine

Change the temperature of water:

Solid (Ice): The particles just shake in place.

{{QUIZ_q5}}

sections.title: 6. Thermal expansion: Everything expands!

quizzes.question: Why do bridges made of concrete and steel have to have small grooves (joints)?

answers.text: So that the rainwater can drain away better.
answers.feedback: No. Drainage is not the main reason; the bridge needs room to change length.

answers.text: So that the bridge has room to expand in the hot summer without breaking.
answers.feedback: Correct: heat expands concrete and steel, and joints prevent damage.

sections.content:
Because the particles wobble faster when heated, they need more space to "dance". The result: Objects expand when they get hot! This happens with solid things, with liquids and with gases. When it gets cold, they contract again.

📖 The Thermometer Secret
Old thermometers use exactly this trick. At the bottom is a red liquid (often alcohol). When it gets warm outside, the red liquid expands and rises up the thin glass tube. We read the temperature!

🌡️ The Thermometer Laboratory

Heat the thermometer with the regulator and see what happens!

{{QUIZ_q6}}

questions.question: 1. Basically, what is “heat” at a microscopic level?

answers.text: The constant movement and trembling of the smallest particles.
answers.feedback: Correct: heat means motion of the smallest particles.

answers.text: Invisible hot rays in the air.
answers.feedback: Not quite: heat is mainly particle motion, not hot air rays.

questions.question: 2. What happens to the particles of a substance when you cool it down significantly?

answers.feedback: No. When cooled, particles move more slowly; they do not burst.
Correct: colder means slower particle motion.

questions.question: 3. At what temperature is the “absolute zero point” at which particles no longer move?

answers.feedback: No. 0 degrees Celsius is only the freezing point of water.
Correct: absolute zero is about -273.15 degrees Celsius.

questions.question: 4. When heat travels through a solid object (like a metal rod), is it called...?

answers.feedback: No. Radiation does not need a solid object; in a metal rod it is conduction.
Correct: heat travels through a solid by conduction.

questions.question: 5. Which material is a particularly GOOD heat conductor?

answers.feedback: Correct: metal conducts heat especially well.
Not quite: wood conducts heat poorly and acts more like an insulator.

questions.question: 6. What do you call materials that conduct heat very POORLY (e.g. Styrofoam, air)?

answers.feedback: No. Generators produce electricity; poor heat conductors are called insulators.
Correct: insulators pass heat on only poorly.

questions.question: 7. How does the sun's heat reach us on Earth through the vacuum of space?

answers.feedback: Correct: heat radiation can travel through a vacuum.
No. In a vacuum, there are no particles to conduct heat from one to another.

questions.question: 8. Which color heats up faster in the sun because it absorbs the light?

answers.feedback: Correct: black absorbs a lot of light and warms up faster.
No. White reflects a lot of light and usually stays cooler.

questions.question: 9. What happens to warm air in a room or hot air balloon?

answers.text: It is lighter and rises upwards (convection).
answers.feedback: Correct: warm air is less dense and rises.

answers.text: She becomes as heavy as lead and falls to the ground.
answers.feedback: No. Warm air does not become heavier; it rises.

questions.question: 10. A snowman melts. Which physical state change takes place?

answers.feedback: No. Liquid turning into gas is called evaporation.
Correct: melting means changing from solid to liquid.

questions.question: 11. What is the process called when water vapor cools and becomes water droplets on the mirror?

answers.feedback: Correct: during condensation, gas becomes liquid again.
No. Freezing is liquid to solid, not gas to water droplets.

questions.question: 12. What do most solid substances do when heated strongly?

answers.feedback: No. Most solids expand when heated.
Correct: heat makes many solids need more space.

questions.question: 13. Why does the red liquid in the thermometer rise as it gets warmer?

answers.text: Because the liquid expands due to the heat and is pushed up in the pipe.
answers.feedback: Correct: the liquid expands and rises in the thin tube.

answers.text: Because little pumps in the tip attract them.
answers.feedback: No. There are no pumps in a thermometer; heat expands the liquid.

questions.question: 14. How does a thick winter jacket protect you from getting cold?

answers.text: It produces hot thermal radiation itself.
answers.feedback: No. The jacket does not make heat; it traps warm air.

answers.text: It traps air pockets, and still air is a great heat insulator.
answers.feedback: Correct: air pockets conduct heat poorly and keep you warm.

questions.question: 15. When you warm your cold hands with a warm cup of tea in winter - which principle do you mainly use?

answers.text: Conduction (the heat travels from the cup into your skin).
answers.feedback: Correct: heat moves by touch from the cup into your hand.
Not mainly. Convection is heat flow in air or liquid.

dgb_word_werkstatt.title: 📝 Word workshop: Write and design documents
dgb_word_werkstatt.subtitle: Self-employed step-by-step tasks for Microsoft Word

sections.title: 1. Orientation: Where is what in Word?
sections.content:
This is what you can do after this workshop:
  • create, save and find a new Word document
  • securely mark, move, copy and format text
  • Headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, images, page numbers and Use headers/footers
  • deliver a finished document as a PDF

Always work like this: read - try it out in Word - check - only then move on. If your Word looks a little different, first look for the same word in the ribbon at the top: Start, Insert, Layout or Check.

Important: You can find most commands at the top of the menu ribbon. First you click on a tab like Home or Insert. Then select the appropriate command in the bar below.

Mini task 1: Reading Word window

  1. Open Microsoft Word and start with Blank Document.
  2. Point your finger or mouse at the tabs File, Start, Insert, Layout and Review.
  3. Click on Start. Find the areas Font, Paragraph and Format templates.
  4. Click once in the white page and write: I working with Word today.
How to control yourself: You see a sentence on the white page and the tab Start is open at the top.
If the ribbon is gone

Press Ctrl + F1 or double-click a tab like Start. Then the bar will appear again.

{{QUIZ_word_q1}}

quizzes.question: Where do you find the most commands in Word?

answers.feedback: Correct. First select tab, then search for command.

answers.text: Only at the bottom of the status bar
answers.feedback: For example, below it says Page, Words and Zoom. Most of the commands are above.
You write on the white page. The commands are at the top.

sections.title: 2. Create a file, save it and find it again
sections.content:
Save is the most important rule. Save early and then repeatedly with Ctrl + S.

File>Save under>Browse>folder select>Write file name>Save

Mini task 2: Save first document

  1. Open a new blank Word document.
  2. Write above: Word workshop by first name last name.
  3. Click on the top left File.
  4. Click Save as. Choose your school folder or the folder that the teacher specifies.
  5. Write as file name: Word_Werkstatt_Firstname_Lastname. Do not use special characters.
  6. Click Save. Then press Ctrl + S.
How to control yourself: Your file name is at the top of the title bar. If you close Word and reopen it, you will find the file in the selected folder.
File name rule: Good file names are short and clear: Fach_Topic_Name. Example: DGB_Word_AminaK.

Mini task 3: Reopen file

  1. Only close Word when your document is saved.
  2. Open Word again.
  3. Click on File > Open.
  4. Select Recently or Browse.
  5. Open your file and write today's below it Date.
How to control yourself: The old file opens and your new date set remains saved after Ctrl + S.
{{QUIZ_word_q2}}

quizzes.question: Which keyboard shortcut saves quickly?

answers.feedback: Exactly. S for Save.
Ctrl + Z undoes the last step.
Ctrl + F searches text in the document.

sections.title: 3. Write, highlight and improve text
sections.content:
Almost everything in Word only works if you mark the correct text . Marking means: The text is highlighted in color and Word knows what you want to change.

Marking a word:
Double-click on the word.
A sentence or range mark:
Drag over the text with the left mouse button pressed.
Mark all:
Ctrl + A.
Reset error:
Ctrl + Z.

Mini task 4: Practice marking

  1. Write these three lines in your document:
    My favorite subject is ...
    I'm learning Word step by step.
    In the end I can I can design a nice document.
  2. Select only the word Word with a double click.
  3. Press Ctrl + C, go to the end of the next line and press Ctrl + V.
  4. Select the inserted text again and delete it with the Delete key.
  5. Do the last step with Ctrl + Z undo.
How to control yourself: You can highlight, copy, paste, delete and restore a single word.
Key tricks: Ctrl + C = copy, Ctrl + V = paste, Ctrl + X = cut, Ctrl + Z = undo, Ctrl + A = select all.

sections.title: 4. Design font: bold, size, color
sections.content:
Font design can be found on the Start tab in the Font section. Always mark text first, then design.

Start>Font>Bold / Italic / Underlined>Font size>Font color

Mini task 5: Design a profile

  1. Write the headline: My profile. Mark them.
  2. Click Start. In the Font area, select: Size 20, Bold, Font Color Blue.
  3. Write four below Lines: Name, class, favorite food, favorite place in Vienna.
  4. Mark only the words Name, Class, Favorite food, Favorite location and make it bold.
  5. Highlight a sentence that you find particularly important and give it a different font color.
How to control yourself: The heading is big and blue. The keywords on the left are bold, but the answers remain readable.
Professional Rule: Use a maximum of two fonts and a maximum of three colors. A document should look clear, not like a poster with too many effects.
{{QUIZ_word_q3}}

quizzes.question: What do you do first before making a text bold or blue?

answers.feedback: Exactly. Word needs to know which text should be changed.
Then you cannot format the text.
It is only printed at the end.

sections.title: 5. Paragraphs: alignment, spacing, lists
sections.content:
A paragraph is a piece of text between two Enter keys. You create paragraphs on Start in the area Paragraph.

Start>Paragraph>Bullets>Numbering>Center>Line- and paragraph spacing

Mini task 6: Building a clean list

  1. Write the heading: My school supplies.
  2. Press enter and write among themselves: notebook, pen, ruler, snack, drinking bottle.
  3. Mark these five Words.
  4. Click Home > Paragraph > Bullets.
  5. Highlight the heading and click Center.
  6. Select the list and open Line and paragraph spacing. Select 1.15 or 1.5.
How to control yourself: The heading is in the middle. The school supplies are presented as a list with points and enough space for reading.

Mini task 7: Write numbered instructions

  1. Write the heading: How to save correctly.
  2. Write these steps underneath, each step on its own line: Click file, select Save as, search for folder, write file name, save click.
  3. Mark the five steps.
  4. Click Start > Paragraph > Numbering.
  5. Check: The steps must be numbered from 1 to 5 be.
How to control yourself: Your instructions have a correct order. Numbers are used when the order is important.

sections.title: 6. Headings and styles
sections.content:
Styles are ready-made text styles. They are better than just changing the size and color by hand every time. Particularly important are Heading 1 and Heading 2.

Start>Styles>Heading 1 or heading 2

Mini task 8: Mini report with real headings

  1. Write as the main heading: My district. Highlight it and choose Start > Styles > Heading 1.
  2. Write below: What I like. Mark this line and select Heading 2.
  3. Write three sentences below about your district.
  4. Afterwards write: What could be better. Vote again Heading 2.
  5. Write two concrete ideas for improvement.
How to control yourself: The main heading looks different than the small subheadings. All headings appear consistent.
Why this is important: With real headings, Word can automatically create a table of contents later. You can also find your way around long texts more quickly.

Mini task 9: Try out the table of contents

  1. Put the cursor at the very beginning of the document.
  2. Press Ctrl + Enter for a new first page.
  3. Click at the top References.
  4. Click Table of Contents and choose an automatic template.
  5. If Word asks if you want to replace the directory, confirm.
How to control yourself: There is a table of contents on page 1. If nothing appears, you probably didn't use heading styles.

sections.title: 7. Page layout: margins, alignment, page breaks
sections.content:
The page layout determines how the sheet is structured. For school assignments Portrait format with normal margins is usually good.

Layout>Borders>Normal
Layout>Orientation>Portrait or landscape

Mini task 10: Start a second page cleanly

  1. Click at the end of your document.
  2. Press Ctrl + Enter. This is a page break.
  3. Write at the top of the new page: My second page.
  4. Click Layout > Margins > Normal.
  5. Click Layout > Orientation > Portrait.
How to control yourself: The second page starts cleanly at the top. You didn't use many enter lines, just a real page break.
Common Error: Many children press Enter 20 times to get to the next page. This will slip later. Use Ctrl + Enter.
instead

sections.title: 8. Insert images and place them correctly
sections.content:
Images make a document clear. What is important is the Text wrapping: It decides whether text can appear next to the image.

Insert>Images>This Device
Click image>Layout options next to the Image>With text in line or square

Mini task 11: Insert image or shape

  1. Click where you want the image to go.
  2. Click Insert > Images > This Device. Choose a picture from your school folder. If you don't have an image: Insert > Shapes and select a rectangle or star.
  3. Click the image. Drag a corner to make it smaller. Don't drag the middle of the page or it will distort.
  4. Click the small icon Layout Options next to the image. Choose With text on line if you want the image to stay like a large letter in the text.
  5. Choose Square if you want text to flow cleanly next to the image should.
How to control yourself: The image is not huge, not distorted and the text does not slip chaotically.
Image rule: For simple school texts, With text in line is safest. For posters and wanted posters, Quadrat is often better.
{{QUIZ_word_q4}}

quizzes.question: What do you drag to make an image smaller without distorting it?

answers.text: At one corner of the picture
answers.feedback: Correct. Corners maintain ratio better.

answers.text: Only in the middle of the left side
answers.feedback: Then the image can become too wide or too narrow.

answers.text: On the text next to it
answers.feedback: The text does not change the image size.

sections.title: 9. Create and organize tables
sections.content:
Tables are good when information belongs in rows and columns: timetable, shopping list, comparison, results list.

Insert>Table>Box mark>z. B. 4 x 5 table

Mini task 12: Timetable table

  1. Click on a free space in the document.
  2. Click Insert > Table. Hover over the boxes and select 4 columns x 5 rows.
  3. Write in the first line: Time, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.
  4. Fill at least three more lines with lessons.
  5. Select the first line and do it bold.
  6. Click on the table. Use Table Design above to choose a simple table style.
How to control yourself: The first line can be recognized as a heading. The table has clear columns and is easier to read than a text list.

Mini task 13: Add row or column

  1. Click in the last row of the table.
  2. Press the Tab key. Word often adds a new line at the end.
  3. Or click in the table and search at the top Table layout > Insert below.
  4. Add a new hour added.
How to control yourself: The table grows in a controlled manner. There are no crooked spaces.

sections.title: 10. Header, footer and page numbers
sections.content:
Headers and footers are outside the normal text. They repeat on every page. Name, class, date or page numbers fit there.

Insert>Header>Empty@@TOKEN_5 5@@
Insert>Since enzahl>End of page

Mini task 14: Header with name

  1. Click on Insert > Header > Blank.
  2. Write in the header: First Name Last Name - Digital Basic education.
  3. Select the text and make it smaller, for example size 10.
  4. Click on top Close header and footer or double click in the normal one Text.
How to control yourself: The name is at the top of every page, but not in the middle of the normal text.

Mini-task 15: Insert page number

  1. Click Insert > Page Number.
  2. Select End of Page and a simple Display.
  3. Close the header/footer view.
  4. Check on page 2 whether there is a page number there.
How to check yourself: Each page automatically has the correct number. You don't have to write the numbers by hand.

sections.title: 11. Spelling, Find and Replace
sections.content:
Word can help with revision. Nevertheless, in the end it is people who decide. Always read your text again out loud or quietly.

Check>Editor or spelling and Grammar
Start>Search

Mini task 16: Consciously improve mistakes

  1. Writing this sentence incorrectly on purpose: I write a document and save it regularly.
  2. Look for red or blue markings under words.
  3. Click along Right-click on a highlighted word and choose a suitable suggestion.
  4. Then click on Check > Editor or Spelling and Grammar.
  5. Improve the sentence until it is correct: I write a document and save it regularly.
How to control yourself: The sentence has been improved. You didn't click blindly, you checked the suggestions.

Mini-Task 17: Find and Replace

  1. In a short paragraph, write the word Handy.
  2. Press Ctrl + H or go to Start > Replace.
  3. Search for Mobile and replace it with Smartphone.
  4. Click first Search so you can see where Word is searching. Then use Replace.
How to check yourself: All appropriate passages have been changed without you having to search through the entire text manually.

sections.title: 12. Submit as PDF and check the finished document
sections.content:
A Word file can sometimes move slightly on other devices. A PDF usually stays the same when opened and printed. PDF is often the safer form for submissions.

File>Save as>File type: PDF>Save
Date i>Print>Preview control

Mini task 18: Create submission file

  1. First save the Word file with Ctrl + S.
  2. Click File > Save at.
  3. Select PDF as the file type. If you can't find this selection: Click File > Export > Create PDF/XPS.
  4. Name the file: DGB_Word_Werkstatt_Firstname_Lastname.pdf.
  5. Open the PDF file briefly and check: Heading, image, table, page numbers and name are visible.
This is how you control yourself: You have two files: a Word file to continue working on and a PDF file to submit.

Submission checklist

  • File name contains subject, topic and name.
  • Heading is clear and not closed colorful.
  • At least one list is properly formatted.
  • At least one table is clearly readable.
  • An image or a shape is appropriately inserted and not distorted.
  • Header or footer contains name/class.
  • Page numbers are inserted automatically.
  • Spelling has been checked.
  • PDF has been opened and controlled.

sections.title: 13. Final project: Design an information sheet
sections.content:
Finally, you connect everything into a real product. Create a one-page or two-page information sheet. Topic: A place in Vienna that young people should know.

Project assignment

  1. Create a new document and save it as DGB_InfoBlatt_Firstname_Lastname.
  2. Write a main heading with Heading 1.
  3. Write a short introductory text with 3 to 5 Sentences.
  4. Insert two subheadings with Heading 2: Why the place is interesting and What to pay attention to there should.
  5. Create a list with at least 4 points.
  6. Insert a table with at least 3 columns: Information, Example, Important.
  7. Insert an image or a shape and carefully adjust the text wrapping.
  8. Insert a header with name and class.
  9. Insert page numbers a.
  10. Check spelling and also save as PDF.

Merksatz: A good Word document is not just beautiful. It is stored, clear, readable, controlled and easy for others to open.
{{QUIZ_word_q5}}

answers.text: Because the layout usually stays the same on other devices
answers.feedback: Exactly. PDF is good for submitting and printing.

answers.text: Because you can continue working in it better than in Word
answers.feedback: The Word file is better for further work. PDF is particularly good for submission.

sections.title: 3. Thunder & Lightning (The Thunderstorm)

quizzes.question: What causes lightning in a cloud?

answers.feedback: Correct: Friction in the cloud separates charges and can trigger lightning.

answers.text: The light of the sun is reflected in the rain.
answers.feedback: Reflective sunlight does not produce lightning. Lightning is an electrical discharge.

sections.content:
Things get wild in a storm cloud! Ice crystals and water droplets swirl around and rub against each other. This creates electric charges (just like when you run across a carpet in your socks).

At some point the tension is so great that it bursts into a huge spark: the lightning. The air expands like lightning - we hear this as Thunder.

sections.title: 4. Precipitation: From rain to hail

quizzes.question: How does hail form?

answers.text: Raindrops are repeatedly thrown up in a thundercloud by strong updrafts and freeze into ice balls.
answers.feedback: Correct: updrafts cause ice grains to grow until they fall as hail.

answers.text: Small snowflakes melt on the way down and immediately freeze on the cold ground.
answers.feedback: That more accurately describes freezing rain. Hail grows above in storm clouds.

sections.content:
Not every drop that falls from a cloud arrives on Earth as liquid rain. What happens depends on the temperature of the layers of air through which it falls!
