sections.title: 5. The conveyor belts of the oceans (ocean currents)

quizzes.question: What properties make water heavier, causing it to sink into the ocean?

answers.feedback: Correct: Cold, salty water is denser and sinks.

answers.text: Warmth and fresh water (from melting glaciers).
answers.feedback: Warm or sweet water is easier. It sinks more slowly and slows down currents.

quizzes.question: What is the name of the warm ocean current that brings mild winters to Europe?

answers.feedback: Correct: The Gulf Stream brings warm water to Europe.
The Humboldt Current lies on the Pacific off South America. Europe is warmed by the Gulf Stream.

sections.content:
Weather is not only created in the air, but also in the water! The world's oceans are connected to each other by huge "conveyor belts". They transport warm water masses from the tropics to cold regions and vice versa.

The engine for these currents is called thermohaline circulation (thermo = temperature, halin = salinity):

  • Salty, cold water is heavy! It sinks into the depths at the poles and flows along the seabed towards the equator.
  • Warm, less salty water is light! It flows back to the poles on the surface as compensation.

🌊 The Gulf Stream: Europe's heating

Click on the button to see how the Gulf Stream works:

Without the warm Gulf Stream from the Caribbean, winter in Europe would be freezing cold (similar to Canada at the same latitude).

{{QUIZ_wetter_s5_q1}} {{QUIZ_wetter_s5_q2}}

questions.question: Which unit measures wind speed?

answers.feedback: Correct: Wind speed can be specified in m/s or km/h.
Hectopascal measures air pressure, not the speed of the wind.

questions.question: Why do we only hear thunder after lightning?

answers.text: Light is much faster than sound.
answers.feedback: Correct: That's why you see lightning before you hear thunder.
Lightning and thunder occur almost simultaneously. The sound just takes longer to reach you.

questions.question: What does a hygrometer measure?

answers.feedback: Correct: A hygrometer measures how much water vapor is in the air.
Temperature is measured by a thermometer. The hygrometer measures air humidity.

questions.question: In a high pressure area...

answers.text: ...the air sinks and it is mostly sunny.
answers.feedback: Correct: sinking air inhibits cloud formation, so it is often friendly.
Rising air is more consistent with low pressure. At high pressure, air sinks.

questions.question: What factors drive global ocean currents at depth?

answers.feedback: Correct: Heat and salinity determine the density of seawater.
Ebb and flow move water briefly. The major upheaval depends primarily on temperature and salt.

klima.title: 🌍 Climate: The big systems 🌡️
klima.subtitle: Climate is not the same as weather. While the weather changes hourly, the climate changes over decades.

sections.title: 1. Weather vs. Climate

quizzes.question: Over what period of time do we look at the weather elements to talk about climate?

answers.feedback: Correct: Climate describes average values ​​over a long period of time, usually 30 years.
Three days show weather, but no climate yet. Climate needs many years of data.

sections.content:
A famous saying goes: "Climate is what you expect, weather is what you get."

We divide the earth into different climate zones:

  • ❄️ Polar Zone: Cold and dry (Arctic/Antarctic).
  • 🌲 Temperate zone: Four seasons (Central Europe).
  • ☀️ Subtropics & Tropics: Hot, often humid (rainforest) or very dry (deserts).
{{QUIZ_klima_s1_q1}}

sections.title: 2. The greenhouse effect

quizzes.question: Without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth would...

answers.feedback: Correct: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the earth would be much colder on average.
The natural greenhouse effect warms the earth. Without him she wouldn't be hotter, but colder.

sections.content:
Our atmosphere seems like a glass house. Gases like CO2 (carbon dioxide) and Methane let in sunlight but trap heat that radiates back from the ground.

🌡️ Greenhouse model

Increase the CO2 concentration and monitor the temperature:

Current temperature: 15.0 °C

{{QUIZ_klima_s2_q1}}

sections.title: 3. Factors affecting the climate

quizzes.question: Why is it usually colder on a mountain than in a valley?

answers.text: Because of the altitude. The air becomes thinner and can store less heat.
answers.feedback: Correct: The temperature usually decreases with altitude.

answers.text: Because mountains are closer to the stars.
answers.feedback: The stars are far too far away. The thinner air at high altitudes is crucial.

quizzes.question: How does the sea influence the climate on the coast?

answers.text: Water retains heat well. It makes winters milder and summers cooler.
answers.feedback: Correct: Oceans equalize temperatures and make coastal climates milder.

answers.text: It makes the climate extremely hot and dry.
answers.feedback: Oceans usually have a balancing effect. Extreme heat and drought are more suited to inland locations or deserts.

sections.content:
The climate in a place is determined by several important factors:

  • 🌍 Geographic latitude: At the equator the sun shines steeply down from above (hot). At the poles the sun's rays hit very flatly and hardly provide any warmth (cold).
  • ⛰️ Altitude: The further up you go (e.g. up a mountain), the colder it gets (around 0.6°C per 100 meters).
  • 🌊 Proximity to the sea: Water warms up slowly, but also cools down slowly. Coasts therefore often have mild winters and moderately warm summers (marine climate). Inland, far from the sea, there are hot summers and icy winters (continental climate).
  • 🏔️ Mountains (windward & leeward): When clouds hit a mountain range, they have to rise and rain falls (windward side). On the other side (leeward) there is only dry wind.
{{QUIZ_klima_s3_q1}} {{QUIZ_klima_s3_q2}}

sections.title: 4. Read climate diagrams

quizzes.question: On a climate diagram it means 'arid (dry) climate' if...

answers.text: ...the precipitation columns lie below the temperature curve.
answers.feedback: Correct: Then more water evaporates than is replaced by precipitation.
Below 0°C means frost. You can recognize the dry season by the ratio of rain and temperature.

sections.content:
To understand the climate of a place at a glance, geographers use climate diagrams. They show average values over many years.

  • 🔴 The red curve: Shows the temperature (in °C).
  • 🟦 The blue bars: Show the precipitation (in mm, which corresponds to liters per square meter).

📊 Interactive climate diagram (example: Rome, Italy)

Hover over the months (or tap) to see the exact values:

Choose a month!

Rule: If the temperature curve (red) is above the precipitation columns (blue), more water evaporates than rains. There is dry season (arid climate). Does Rome experience a dry season in summer?

{{QUIZ_klima_s4_q1}}

sections.title: 5. The journey through time of climate research

quizzes.question: What do ice cores from Antarctica tell us?

answers.text: They contain tiny, ancient air bubbles that allow us to measure the composition of the atmosphere thousands of years ago.
answers.feedback: That's right: air bubbles in the ice are an archive of the previous atmosphere.

answers.text: They show us whether fish used to live in the ice.
answers.feedback: Ice cores examine the air and climate, not fish tracks in the ice.

sections.content:
Weather recordings with thermometers have only been around for about 150 years. But how do researchers know how hot it was 10,000 years ago? You use Climate Archives of nature!

🔬 The Climate Archive

Select an archive to find out more!
{{QUIZ_klima_s5_q1}}

questions.question: Which gas is a major greenhouse gas?

answers.feedback: Correct: CO2 is an important greenhouse gas.
Nitrogen is the main component of air, but is not an important greenhouse gas like CO2.

questions.question: What happens if the greenhouse effect gets stronger?

answers.feedback: Correct: A stronger greenhouse effect keeps more heat in the atmosphere.
This does not change the color of the sun. More greenhouse gases retain more heat.

questions.question: How does proximity to the ocean usually affect the climate?

answers.feedback: That's right: the sea stores heat and balances the seasons.
Such strong contrasts are more typical far away from the sea.

questions.question: How do we know how warm it was thousands of years ago?

answers.text: Through ice cores and tree rings
answers.feedback: That's right: Natural archives show evidence of past climates.
Weather apps have only been around for a short time. Natural archives are used for ancient times.

klimawandel.title: 🆘 Climate Change: The Crisis 🧊
klimawandel.subtitle: By burning coal, oil and gas we increase the greenhouse effect. The earth is getting too hot too quickly.

sections.title: 1. Why is it getting warmer?
sections.content:
For millions of years, nature has buried CO2 in the ground in the form of plant residues. This became coal, petroleum and natural gas. If we burn these today, we will blow all the stored CO2 into the air.

The result: The "blanket" around the earth is getting thicker and it's getting warmer.

{{QUIZ_kw_s1_q1}}

quizzes.question: What happens when fossil fuels are burned?

answers.text: CO2 is released that was previously stored for millions of years.
answers.feedback: Correct: When burned, long-stored carbon is released into the air as CO2.

answers.text: Oxygen is created, which cools the atmosphere.
answers.feedback: When burning, oxygen is consumed, not created. This creates CO2, which warms.
Air pollution is its own problem. Climate change is primarily exacerbated by greenhouse gases.

sections.title: 2. The consequences
sections.content:
Warming has dramatic consequences:

  • 🏔️ Ice melting: Glaciers and the ice at the poles are melting.
  • 🌊 Sea level rise: Coastal cities are in danger.
  • 🌪️ Extreme weather: More droughts, but also more severe storms and floods.

🧊 The Time Travel Ice Melt

Move the year and watch the ice:

{{QUIZ_kw_s2_q1}}

quizzes.question: Why are sea levels rising?

answers.text: Glacier ice melts and water expands when warm.
answers.feedback: Correct: Both cause sea levels to rise.
More rain is not the main reason. Melting land ice and warmer sea water are crucial.

answers.text: Because thermometers don't work in winter.
answers.feedback: Thermometers also work in winter. You have to classify the data correctly.

sections.title: 3. What can we do?
sections.content:
Every contribution counts! We have to stop CO2 emissions. This is called Climate Protection.

  • ☀️ Renewable energies: Sun and wind instead of coal.
  • 🚲 Mobility: More bikes and trains, less cars and planes.
  • 🥦 Nutrition: Regional and plant-based foods often use less CO2.
🌍 Research task: Search the Internet for the “CO2 footprint calculator”. Try to find out how much CO2 your lifestyle causes per year. What is your greatest position? (Tip: Most of the time it is housing, mobility or nutrition).

quizzes.question: Why can drought stress increase even though summer precipitation is not clearly decreasing everywhere?

answers.text: Because higher temperatures cause more evaporation.
answers.feedback: Correct. Heat removes more water from soil and plants.

answers.text: Because rain in Austria no longer consists of water.
answers.feedback: No. The decisive factors are temperature, evaporation and distribution of rain.
That is not the explanation. It's all about heat and evaporation.

sections.title: 4. How far have we come? (The temperature limit)
sections.content:
In order to prevent the worst catastrophes, almost all countries in the world have agreed: The earth must not warm up more than 1.5 °C compared to the time before large factories (pre-industrial period) !

🌡️ The Danger Thermometer

Where are we currently compared to the limit?

0.0°C: Normal state (before 1850)

~1.2°C: Our current status today! We are already feeling significantly more heat waves and heavy rain.

1.5°C: The absolute limit. If it gets warmer, there is a risk of irreversible consequences (tipping points).

{{QUIZ_kw_s4_q1}}

quizzes.question: What maximum warming limit did the countries agree on in the Paris Climate Agreement?

answers.feedback: Correct: The Paris Agreement aims to limit warming to 1.5 °C if possible.
5°C would be very dangerous and is not the agreed limit. The goal is 1.5 °C if possible.
This is, above all, climate protection.

sections.title: 5. The dominoes of the earth (tipping points)
sections.content:
Imagine leaning further and further back on a chair. Nothing happens for a long time, but suddenly you reach a point where you inevitably fall backwards. This is a tipping point.

There are tipping points like this in our climate. When they fall, they trigger a chain reaction (like dominoes) that we humans can no longer stop.

🧨 The Tipping Point Chain Reaction

Click on the first domino to see what could happen if we ignore the limit:

1. Greenland ice is melting 🧊
Fresh water flows into the ocean.
2. Gulf Stream stops 🌊
The low-salinity water is too light to sink. The current stops.
3. Amazon dries up 🌳
Without the current, the rain in South America changes. The rainforest is dying.
4. Permafrost is thawing 🌫️
Nature no longer stores CO2. Methane escapes -> Earth overheats!

💥 When the first stone falls, we can't stop the rest!

{{QUIZ_kw_s5_q1}}

quizzes.question: What happens if the permafrost in Siberia thaws?

answers.text: It releases huge amounts of the greenhouse gas methane, which heats the earth even faster.
answers.feedback: Correct: Thawing permafrost can release methane and increase warming.
Thawing does not immediately mean a tropical climate. What is important is that methane can be released.

answers.text: Tipping points have nothing to do with temperature.
answers.feedback: But. The level of warming influences many risks.

sections.title: 6. From knowledge to action
sections.content:
Climate change is not an issue for which individual children bear all responsibility. But knowledge helps to understand and have a say in good decisions: at school, at home, in the community and later as adults.

I can:
Turn off devices, plan routes, fix things, not waste food, facts check.
We as a class can:
Create heat rules, map shaded areas, examine waste and energy consumption, suggest school gardens/trees.
Politics and economics have to:
Convert energy, transport, buildings, industry and agriculture so that much fewer greenhouse gases are produced.
Mini project: Choose a location in your school. Note: Where is it too hot in summer? What would climate protection be? What would be adaptation? Draw a simple improvement idea.
Sources for teachers: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report, NASA Climate Evidence, GeoSphere Austria: Air temperature, GeoSphere Austria: FAQ.

questions.question: What are fossil fuels?

answers.feedback: Correct: These fuels were created from very old plant and animal remains.
Wind is not a fuel, and wood is not a fossil fuel like coal, oil or natural gas.

questions.question: What is the effect called when white ice reflects sunlight?

answers.feedback: Correct: Bright surfaces reflect a lot of sunlight.
That describes the effect, but is not the technical term. The term is called the albedo effect.

questions.question: What limit have the states agreed on?

answers.feedback: Correct: States want to limit warming to 1.5 °C if possible.
4 °C is not a protection limit. It was agreed to stay well below this and aim for 1.5 °C.

questions.question: What is a climate tipping point?

answers.text: A threshold that, when exceeded, triggers unstoppable chain reactions.
answers.feedback: Correct: After a tipping point, a system itself can continue to change.

answers.text: A place in the Arctic Circle where the thermometer tips.
answers.feedback: A tipping point is not a place. It is a critical threshold in the climate system.

geo_oesterreich_alltag.title: 🗺️ Austria in Everyday Life
geo_oesterreich_alltag.subtitle: Orientation, federal states, and everyday routes in Austria.

sections.title: 1. Where am I?
sections.content:
Goal: You can find Austria on a map and describe where you are in simple words.

Austria is in Europe. It has nine federal states. Geography helps in daily life: on the way to school, at a doctor appointment, while shopping, when meeting friends, or when looking for an address.

Everyday life: If you say, "I am at the stop in front of the park," someone can find you more easily than if you say, "I am somewhere outside."
Remember: A map shows a place from above. On many maps, north is at the top. A local map often shows a small area, such as one district.
Common mix-up: "Austria" is the country. "Vienna", "Tyrol" and "Styria" are federal states. A street or a stop is smaller.
  • Micro task 1: Name a real start point and destination for today.
  • Micro task 2: Write down three landmarks: a street, stop, shop, park, school or bridge.
  • Micro task 3: Draw a mini-map with your school, the nearest stop and a safe crossing.
Transfer: A new student asks for the way from the school gate to the office. Explain the route in four short sentences with a start, a destination, a direction and one landmark.
{{QUIZ_geo_q1}}

quizzes.question: What helps you find your way in a new district?

answers.text: Street names, stops and clear landmarks.
answers.feedback: Correct: These points help you describe a route clearly.

answers.text: Only the color of a house.
answers.feedback: A house color can change. Street names and stops are safer.

sections.title: 2. City, Country, River
sections.content:
Austria has large cities, small towns, mountains, valleys, lakes and rivers. Vienna is the largest city. The Danube is an important river. Many Austrian mountains are in the Alps. Federal states divide Austria into large areas.

Everyday life: Weather, traffic and leisure plans depend on the area. There may be snow in the mountains while it rains in Vienna. Near rivers, people watch flood warnings after heavy rain.
Remember: City, river, mountain and federal state are different categories. A clear answer names the right category.
Common misconception: The Danube is not a federal state. Tyrol is not a river. Vienna is both a city and a federal state.
  • Micro task 1: Match: Danube = river, Alps = mountains, Vienna = city/federal state.
  • Micro task 2: Name one federal state and one city you know.
  • Micro task 3: Explain the difference between a city and a federal state with an example.
Transfer: Plan a class trip to another federal state. Which three facts do you need? Think about route, weather and costs.
{{QUIZ_geo_q2}}

quizzes.question: What is the Danube?

answers.feedback: Exactly: The Danube is a river and also flows through Vienna.
Not quite: A federal state is, for example, Vienna, Tyrol or Styria.

sections.title: 3. My Route with Public Transport
sections.content:
Geography helps with routes. You read stops, line numbers, directions and transfer points. The key question is: Which direction does this line go? The same line can travel in two directions.

Everyday life: If you need to get to training, an office or a hospital, check the start, destination and transfer first. That saves stress.
Remember: A route needs a start, a destination, a line, a direction and sometimes a transfer.
Common misconception: The line number alone is not enough. A line often goes out and back. The direction tells you whether you are boarding the right vehicle.
  1. Micro task 1: Write a route as a chain: start -> line -> transfer -> destination.
  2. Micro task 2: Mark the departure time, direction and final stop on a timetable.
  3. Micro task 3: Name two reasons to leave earlier than the timetable suggests.
Transfer: Your phone battery is empty. Describe how you can still get home with stop signs and a route map.
{{QUIZ_geo_q3}}

quizzes.question: What must you check especially with underground, bus or tram?

answers.feedback: Correct: The same line can travel in two directions.

answers.text: Only the color of the seats.
answers.feedback: The seats do not help with the route. Line, stop and direction matter.

questions.question: What belongs in a good route description?

answers.text: Start, destination and important points on the way.
answers.feedback: Exactly: Then another person can follow the route.
That is too unclear. A route description needs start and destination.

questions.question: What is Vienna?

answers.text: A city and a federal state.
answers.feedback: Correct: Vienna is both.
Vienna is in eastern Austria and is not a mountain.

chemie_alltag_stoffe.title: 🧪 Substances in Everyday Life
chemie_alltag_stoffe.subtitle: Everyday chemistry starts with water, salt, air, soap and safe choices.

sections.title: 1. What is a substance?
sections.content:
Goal: You can recognize substances and describe simple properties.

A substance is a material. Water, air, salt, sugar, iron, plastic and glass are substances. Objects are made from substances. A drinking bottle can be made of plastic or metal. A window is made of glass and frame material.

Everyday life: When you shop, cook or clean, you compare substances: Is it solid or liquid? Does it smell strong? Does it dissolve in water? Could it be harmful?
Remember: You recognize substances by properties such as color, smell, state, hardness, solubility, magnetism or flammability.
Common misconception: In chemistry, "substance" does not only mean cloth. Water, air and salt are substances too.
  • Micro task 1: Name three substances from your school bag.
  • Micro task 2: Describe water with three properties.
  • Micro task 3: Decide: glass, sugar, air - solid, liquid or gas?
Transfer: You want to choose a lunch box. Which material properties matter? Think about weight, cleaning, breaking and contact with food.
{{QUIZ_ch_q1}}

quizzes.question: What is a substance?

answers.text: A material that things are made of.
answers.feedback: Correct: Water, glass and iron are examples of substances.

answers.text: Only something dangerous in a lab.
answers.feedback: Not every substance is dangerous. You use many substances every day.

sections.title: 2. Mixing and Separating
sections.content:
Many everyday things are mixtures. Cocoa is milk mixed with cocoa powder. Salt water is water with dissolved salt. Soil contains sand, small stones and plant parts. Sometimes you can separate a mixture again.

Everyday life: A pasta sieve separates pasta from water. A coffee filter holds back coffee grounds. Recycling also separates materials.
Remember: Sieving separates large and small solid pieces. Filtering separates solid particles from a liquid. Evaporation can leave a dissolved substance behind.
Common misconception: When salt "disappears" in water, it is not gone. It is dissolved. Evaporation can make it visible again.
  • Micro task 1: Choose the method: separate sand and stones - sieve or stir?
  • Micro task 2: Explain why a filter is not enough for salt water.
  • Micro task 3: Name one mixture from the kitchen.
Transfer: After sports, soil is in a drinking cup. Plan a safe separation. What works with a filter, and what does not?
{{QUIZ_ch_q2}}

quizzes.question: How can you separate sand from water?

answers.feedback: Exactly: Sand stays in the filter, water runs through.
Stirring spreads the sand. A filter separates sand and water better.

sections.title: 3. Safe with Chemistry
sections.content:
Chemistry is not only a laboratory subject. Detergent, batteries, deodorant, glue and cleaning products are part of chemistry too. Some substances can harm skin, eyes, breathing or the environment. That is why we read warning symbols and work calmly.

Everyday life: Toilet cleaner, descaler and bleach must not be poured together. Dangerous fumes can form.
Remember: Read the label first, then act. Do not taste, directly smell or mix unknown substances.
Common misconception: More cleaner is not automatically better. Too much cleaner, or the wrong mixture, can be dangerous.
  1. Micro task 1: Name two safety rules for everyday chemistry.
  2. Micro task 2: Find a warning symbol on a package and describe it.
  3. Micro task 3: Practise a help sentence: "I spilled ...".
Transfer: An unknown cleaner has spilled at home. What do you do first, second and third?
{{QUIZ_ch_q3}}

quizzes.question: Why should you not simply mix cleaning products?

answers.text: Dangerous substances or fumes can form.
answers.feedback: Correct: Some mixtures are dangerous for eyes, skin or breathing.

answers.text: Because then the bottle becomes heavier.
answers.feedback: The weight is not the problem. Dangerous reactions are the problem.

questions.question: Which property can you observe with sugar?

answers.feedback: Correct: Sugar is soluble in water.
Sugar is not attracted by a magnet.

questions.question: What do you do with an unknown substance?

answers.text: Do not taste, do not mix, ask an adult.
answers.feedback: Exactly: Safety comes first.
That is dangerous. Unknown substances are not tasted.

bio_koerper_gesundheit.title: 🫀 Body & Health
bio_koerper_gesundheit.subtitle: Food, breathing, movement and protection in daily life.

sections.title: 1. Your Body Needs Energy
sections.content:
Goal: You can explain why food, water and sleep are important.

Your body works all the time. Even when you sit still, your heart beats. When you learn, your brain needs energy. Food gives energy and building materials. Water helps move substances through the body. Sleep supports recovery and learning.

Everyday life: If someone comes to school without breakfast or a drink, they may become tired, restless or unfocused sooner. A snack and water can help.
Remember: Food gives energy and building materials. Water transports substances. Sleep helps the body recover.
Common misconception: Body energy is not electricity from a socket. Your body gets energy from nutrients.
  • Micro task 1: Match: water, sleep, bread - what helps with what?
  • Micro task 2: Name two signs that your body needs water or a break.
  • Micro task 3: Compare a sweet drink and water. Which is usually more useful at school?
Transfer: Plan a simple snack for a long school day. Explain how it supports energy, water and recovery.
{{QUIZ_bio_q1}}

quizzes.question: Why does your body need food?

answers.feedback: Correct: Food helps with moving, thinking, growing and repairing.
Looks are not the main reason. The body needs energy and building materials.

sections.title: 2. Breathing and Blood Circulation
sections.content:
When you breathe in, oxygen enters the lungs. Blood carries oxygen to muscles and organs. The heart pumps blood through the body. During movement, muscles need more oxygen, so breathing and pulse become faster.

Everyday life: After climbing stairs, running or playing football, you can feel your pulse more clearly. This is a normal reaction to muscle work.
Remember: The lungs take in oxygen. The heart and blood distribute it. Muscles need more oxygen during movement.
Common misconception: Air does not go straight into the muscles. Oxygen moves from the lungs into the blood and is then carried through the body.
  • Micro task 1: Count your pulse for 15 seconds at rest and multiply by 4.
  • Micro task 2: Do 20 squats and compare your pulse.
  • Micro task 3: Describe the path: air -> lungs -> blood -> muscle.
Transfer: Someone gets a side stitch during sport and breathes very fast. Which calm steps can help without causing panic?
{{QUIZ_bio_q2}}

quizzes.question: Why does the heart beat faster during movement?

answers.feedback: Exactly: The blood then brings oxygen to the muscles faster.

answers.text: Because the bones need more space.
answers.feedback: The bones are not the reason. Muscles need more oxygen during movement.

sections.title: 3. Protection: Skin, Hygiene, First Aid
sections.content:
The skin protects your body. Washing hands removes many germs. For a small wound, clean it, cover it with a plaster and watch it. If there is strong pain, heavy bleeding, breathing trouble or unconsciousness, get help immediately.

Everyday life: At school, on public transport and in sports halls, many people touch the same surfaces. Washing hands before eating and after using the toilet lowers the risk of infection.
Remember: Skin protects you. Hygiene reduces germs. In an emergency in Austria, call 144 for an ambulance or 112 for the European emergency number.
Common misconception: Not every germ makes you ill. But dirty hands can bring germs into your mouth, nose or wounds.
  1. Micro task 1: Put these steps in order: wash hands, clean wound, plaster, observe.
  2. Micro task 2: Name two situations when you must get an adult.
  3. Micro task 3: Practise an emergency call sentence: Where? What? How many people? Which injury?
Transfer: Someone falls in the schoolyard and has a bleeding knee. Describe what you do and what you do not do.
{{QUIZ_bio_q3}}

quizzes.question: Why is washing hands useful?

answers.text: It removes many germs from the skin.
answers.feedback: Correct: Fewer germs can reach mouth, nose or wounds.
No: Washing hands mainly helps against germs and dirt.

questions.question: What transports oxygen in the body?

answers.feedback: Correct: Blood brings oxygen to body parts.
Hair does not transport oxygen. Blood does that.

questions.question: What is useful for a small wound?

answers.text: Clean it and use a plaster.
answers.feedback: Exactly: Cleanliness protects the wound.
That can bring germs into the wound. Clean hands matter.

math1_1_vs_wissen.title: Level 1: Defeat elementary school boss 🏆
math1_1_vs_wissen.subtitle: Everything you already know from elementary school!

sections.title: Plus and minus ➕➖
sections.content:
No matter whether it's V-Bucks, Robux or real pocket money: you always need pluses and minuses!

Trainer-Bot:
Calculate: + =

If you calculate Plus it will be more (adding). If you calculate Minus, it becomes less (subtract).

{{QUIZ_m11_q1}}

quizzes.question: You have 50 euros. You buy a game for 20 euros. How many euros do you have left?

answers.feedback: Correct. You apply everyday math correctly.
Not yet. Calculate the amount step by step and check your result.
Not yet. Calculate the amount step by step and check your result.

sections.title: Times and Shares ✖️➗
sections.content:
Imagine you are playing Minecraft and need wood. 1 tree gives 4 wood. How much wood does 5 trees give? Correct: 5 Times 4! (Multiply).

When Divide (Divide) you divide fairly. 20 chicken nuggets for 4 friends? Everyone gets 5!

Trainer Bot:
Calculate: × =
{{QUIZ_m11_q2}}

quizzes.question: You buy 3 kebabs for 5 euros each. How much do you have to pay?

answers.feedback: Correct. You apply everyday math correctly.
Not yet. Calculate the amount step by step and check your result.
Not yet. Calculate the amount step by step and check your result.

questions.question: What does 'divide' mean?

answers.feedback: Correct: Dividing means sharing into equal parts.
Not yet. Think about which basic term fits here.

questions.question: 4 times 6 is...?

answers.feedback: Correct: 4 × 6 equals 24.
Not yet. Think about which basic term fits here.

questions.question: What sign is for minus?

answers.feedback: Correct: The minus sign is "-".
Not yet. Think about which basic term fits here.

sections.title: Digits and numbers
sections.content:
Imagine you are playing a game. Your level is a number. For example: Level 12.

sections.title: 1. Multiplication (multiplication)
sections.content:
2 rows of 3 squares = 2 · 3 = 6

Multiplication is basically a shortened addition (e.g. 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 4). The numbers that are multiplied together are called factors. The result is the Product. So: Factor · Factor = Product.

answers.feedback: Correct: factor × factor gives the product.

sections.title: 2nd Division (Share)
sections.content:
6 divided into 2 groups = 3 each Group

Division is the inverse operation of multiplication. The number that is divided is called Dividend. The number you divide by is called Divisor. The result is called Quotient. Most important rule: You must never divide by zero!

sections.title: 3. Calculation laws and connection of basic arithmetic operations
sections.content:
a · (b + c) = a · b + a · c

The commutative and associative laws also apply to multiplication. In addition, there is the Distributive law (distribution law), which connects multiplication with addition/subtraction. sections.title: Point, line, ray, distance ✏️
sections.content:
Geometry is like drawing according to strict rules. You'll need this to build houses or game levels later!

  • Point: Just a small place. Is named with a capital letter (A, B). In the notebook you make a small cross.
  • Straight: A line that continues infinitely in both directions. Has no beginning and no end. Lowercase letter (g, h).
  • Beam (half-straight): Like a laser beam! Has a beginning, but no end.
  • Rout: Has beginning and end. It is therefore measurable (e.g. 5 cm long). From point A to point B.

quizzes.question: What has a beginning but NO end?

answers.feedback: Correct. A ray starts at one point and extends forever in one direction.
Not quite. A line has no start and no end.

quizzes.question: What can you measure with the ruler?

answers.feedback: Exactly. A segment has two endpoints, and you can measure its length.
Not quite. A line is infinite, so with a ruler you measure segments.

sections.content:

Not quite. A ray has one starting point and extends infinitely in only one direction.

sections.title: What is a fraction?
sections.content:
Imagine you have a delicious pizza and want to share it with your friends. If you cut the pizza into equal pieces, each piece is a fraction (a part) of the whole pizza.

A fraction shows us that something is not whole, but only a part of which.

quizzes.question: What does a fraction indicate?
quizzes.explanation: A fraction always represents a part of a whole when it is divided into equal pieces.

answers.feedback: The size alone is not enough: the fraction describes the proportion of the whole.
Correct: A fraction describes a part of a whole.
The price is not a fraction. A fraction shows a proportion.
A fraction can be finite or infinite as a decimal number, but what is meant is a proportion.

quizzes.question: If you cut a cake into 4 equal pieces, what is 1 piece?
quizzes.explanation: One of four pieces of equal size is called a quarter (1/4).

sections.title: Numerator & denominator
sections.content:
Every fraction has two important numbers separated by a fraction bar:

  • Denominator (bottom): tells how many equal parts the whole is divided into.

answers.feedback: The counter counts parts, not the size of the whole or entire objects.

sections.title: True and improper fractions
sections.content:
There are different types of fractions, depending on how large the numerator and denominator are.

  • Real fraction: The numerator is smaller than the denominator (e.g. 3/4). The fraction is smaller than a whole.
  • Improper fraction: The numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator (e.g. 5/4). The fraction is greater than a whole or exactly a whole.

sections.title: Expand & Shorten (Basics)
sections.content:
Sometimes fractions look different but mean exactly the same thing! This is called Expand or Reduce.

  • Expand: The numerator and denominator are multiplied by the same number (e.g. 1/2 = 2/4). The pieces become smaller, but there are more.
  • Reduce: The numerator and denominator are divided by the same number (e.g. 2/4 = 1/2). You put pieces together.

quizzes.question: What do you have to do when expanding a fraction?

answers.text: Just multiply the denominator by a number

You just doubled the denominator. The counter must also be 2: 2/6.

Shortening is sharing, not simply deleting zeros.
